rules.title: SSH allows root to log in with a password
rules.finding_message: sshd lets root log in with a password (PermitRootLogin yes). Set it to prohibit-password or no, and log in as a named user.
rules.explain: With PermitRootLogin yes, password guessers can aim straight at root: the one account every Linux host has, and the one that controls everything.
rules.check: First make sure a named user can log in and use sudo. In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password`, and change any other PermitRootLogin line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (sshd keeps the first value it reads, and those files come first). Run `sshd -t` to check the syntax, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). `sshd -T | grep -i permitrootlogin` shows the value in effect. `no` is stricter and also fine.

rules.title: SSH accepts passwords
rules.finding_message: sshd accepts password logins (PasswordAuthentication is yes or not set), which password guessing can reach. Use keys and set PasswordAuthentication no.
rules.explain: Passwords can be guessed, phished or reused from other breaches; SSH keys cannot be guessed. Bots try common passwords against every SSH server they find.
rules.check: Install your key (`ssh-copy-id user@host`) and test a key login in a second session, keeping this one open. In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set `PasswordAuthentication no`, and change any other PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (sshd keeps the first value it reads, and those files come first). Run `sshd -t` to check the syntax, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). `sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication` shows the value in effect. Also set `KbdInteractiveAuthentication no`, or PAM can still ask for a password.

rules.title: SSH allows empty passwords
rules.finding_message: sshd lets accounts with an empty password log in (PermitEmptyPasswords yes). Set it to no.
rules.explain: Accounts with an empty password can then log in over SSH with no password at all: anyone who knows the user name gets in.
rules.check: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set `PermitEmptyPasswords no`, and change any other PermitEmptyPasswords line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (sshd keeps the first value it reads, and those files come first). Run `sshd -t` to check the syntax, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). `sshd -T | grep -i permitemptypasswords` shows the value in effect. `awk -F: '$2==""' /etc/shadow` lists accounts with no password.

rules.title: SSH trusts other hosts
rules.finding_message: sshd accepts host-based authentication (HostbasedAuthentication yes): a user trusted on another host logs in here without a password. Set it to no.
rules.explain: Host-based login trusts another machine's word about who a user is. If that machine is taken over, or its identity faked, the attacker gets in here without a password.
rules.check: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set `HostbasedAuthentication no`, and change any other HostbasedAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (sshd keeps the first value it reads, and those files come first). Run `sshd -t` to check the syntax, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). `sshd -T | grep -i hostbasedauthentication` shows the value in effect.

rules.title: SSH reads .rhosts files
rules.finding_message: sshd honours users' .rhosts and .shosts files (IgnoreRhosts no). Set it to yes.
rules.explain: .rhosts and .shosts files let a user name other hosts and users that may log in as them without a password. A user, or an attacker who has their account, can add one quietly.
rules.check: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set `IgnoreRhosts yes`, and change any other IgnoreRhosts line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (sshd keeps the first value it reads, and those files come first). Run `sshd -t` to check the syntax, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). `sshd -T | grep -i ignorerhosts` shows the value in effect. Remove leftover files: `find / /home -xdev \( -name .rhosts -o -name .shosts \)`.

rules.title: SSH lets users set the login environment
rules.finding_message: sshd reads users' ~/.ssh/environment (PermitUserEnvironment yes), which can bypass restrictions such as LD_PRELOAD rules. Set it to no.
rules.explain: Users can then set environment variables such as LD_PRELOAD for their SSH sessions, which can get around restrictions such as forced commands or restricted shells.
rules.check: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set `PermitUserEnvironment no`, and change any other PermitUserEnvironment line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (sshd keeps the first value it reads, and those files come first). Run `sshd -t` to check the syntax, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). `sshd -T | grep -i permituserenvironment` shows the value in effect.

rules.title: SSH allows many login attempts per connection
rules.finding_message: sshd allows more than 4 authentication attempts per connection (MaxAuthTries, default 6). Set MaxAuthTries 4 or lower.
rules.explain: Each SSH connection may try this many passwords or keys. A lower limit slows password guessing and makes repeated failures show in the logs sooner.
rules.check: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set `MaxAuthTries 4`, and change any other MaxAuthTries line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (sshd keeps the first value it reads, and those files come first). Run `sshd -t` to check the syntax, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). `sshd -T | grep -i maxauthtries` shows the value in effect. Users with many keys may need `IdentitiesOnly yes` in their client config.

rules.title: SSH waits long for a login
rules.finding_message: sshd keeps unauthenticated connections open for more than 60 seconds (LoginGraceTime, default 120; 0 is no limit). Set LoginGraceTime 60 or lower.
rules.explain: A connection that has not logged in yet holds one of the server's few login slots (MaxStartups). A long grace time lets an attacker hold many slots open and lock real users out.
rules.check: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set `LoginGraceTime 60`, and change any other LoginGraceTime line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (sshd keeps the first value it reads, and those files come first). Run `sshd -t` to check the syntax, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). `sshd -T | grep -i logingracetime` shows the value in effect.

rules.title: SSH forwards X11
rules.finding_message: sshd forwards X11 (X11Forwarding yes), which exposes the client's display to the server. Set it to no unless people run graphical programs over SSH.
rules.explain: X11 forwarding lets programs on the server open windows on the client's screen. If the server is compromised, it can read the client's keystrokes and screen through that link. Most servers never need it.
rules.check: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set `X11Forwarding no`, and change any other X11Forwarding line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (sshd keeps the first value it reads, and those files come first). Run `sshd -t` to check the syntax, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). `sshd -T | grep -i x11forwarding` shows the value in effect.

rules.title: SSH logs too little
rules.expression: facts['sshd.loglevel'] == 'quiet' || facts['sshd.loglevel'] == 'Quiet' || facts['sshd.loglevel'] == 'QUIET' || facts['sshd.loglevel'] == 'fatal' || facts['sshd.loglevel'] == 'Fatal' || facts['sshd.loglevel'] == 'FATAL' || facts['sshd.loglevel'] == 'error' || facts['sshd.loglevel'] == 'Error' || facts['sshd.loglevel'] == 'ERROR'
rules.finding_message: sshd logs too little to see logins (LogLevel QUIET, FATAL or ERROR). Set LogLevel INFO or VERBOSE.
rules.explain: At QUIET, FATAL or ERROR, sshd does not log successful or failed logins, so password guessing and break-ins leave no trace to investigate.
rules.check: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set `LogLevel INFO`, and change any other LogLevel line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (sshd keeps the first value it reads, and those files come first). Run `sshd -t` to check the syntax, then `systemctl reload sshd` (Debian/Ubuntu: `ssh`). `sshd -T | grep -i loglevel` shows the value in effect. VERBOSE also logs key fingerprints.

rules.title: sshd_config is open to other users
rules.expression: (facts['file.etc_sshd_config.mode'] != '' && facts['file.etc_sshd_config.mode'] != '0600' && facts['file.etc_sshd_config.mode'] != '0640' && facts['file.etc_sshd_config.mode'] != '0400' && facts['file.etc_sshd_config.mode'] != '0440' && !(facts['file.etc_sshd_config.mode'] == '0644' && ('debian' in facts['os.id_like'] || 'ubuntu' in facts['os.id_like'] || 'arch' in facts['os.id_like']))) || (facts['file.etc_sshd_config.owner'] != '' && !facts['file.etc_sshd_config.owner'].startsWith('0:'))
rules.finding_message: /etc/ssh/sshd_config can be read or changed by users other than root (accepted: 0600, 0640 or stricter; also 0644, the stock mode on Debian, Ubuntu and Arch), or is not owned by root. Make it root:root 0600.
rules.explain: sshd_config decides who may log in and how. A user who can change it can let themselves in as root; one who can read it learns the login policy.
rules.check: Run `chown root:root /etc/ssh/sshd_config && chmod 0600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config`. No restart is needed. Check the files in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ the same way.

rules.title: Address space randomisation is weakened
rules.finding_message: kernel.randomize_va_space is not 2, so memory layouts are easier to predict for an exploit. Set it to 2.
rules.explain: Address space layout randomisation (ASLR) places a program's memory at random addresses each run. With it off or partial, an attacker exploiting a memory bug can predict where code and data are, which makes the exploit much more reliable.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w kernel.randomize_va_space=2` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `kernel.randomize_va_space = 2` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'kernel.randomize_va_space' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files.

rules.title: Any process can trace another of the same user
rules.finding_message: kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is 0: any process can attach to another process of the same user and read its memory. Set it to 1.
rules.explain: With ptrace_scope 0, any program you run can attach to your other programs and read their memory, for example an SSH agent or a browser holding passwords. Malware running as a user uses this to steal secrets.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=1` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'kernel.yama.ptrace_scope' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files. Debuggers such as gdb and strace then attach only to their own child processes, or with sudo.

rules.title: Unprivileged users can load BPF programs
rules.finding_message: kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled is 0: any user can load BPF programs, a frequent kernel exploit path. Set it to 1 or 2.
rules.explain: BPF lets programs load small pieces of code into the kernel. When every user may do this, bugs in the kernel's BPF checker become a way to gain root; many kernel exploits have used it.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=2` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 2` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files. 1 also works but cannot be undone without a reboot.

rules.title: Kernel addresses are visible to users
rules.finding_message: kernel.kptr_restrict is 0: kernel pointers are shown to users, which helps kernel exploits. Set it to 1.
rules.explain: Kernel memory addresses in /proc and the logs help an attacker aim a kernel exploit. Hiding them from normal users removes that help at no cost.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w kernel.kptr_restrict=1` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `kernel.kptr_restrict = 1` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'kernel.kptr_restrict' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files.

rules.title: Users can read the kernel log
rules.finding_message: kernel.dmesg_restrict is 0: any user can read the kernel log, including addresses and hardware details. Set it to 1.
rules.explain: The kernel log can show memory addresses, hardware and driver details and other users' activity. Limiting it to administrators keeps that from an attacker who got a normal account.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w kernel.dmesg_restrict=1` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'kernel.dmesg_restrict' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files. Users then read it with `sudo dmesg`.

rules.title: Link protections are off
rules.finding_message: fs.protected_hardlinks or fs.protected_symlinks is 0, which allows link tricks in shared directories such as /tmp. Set both to 1.
rules.explain: In shared folders such as /tmp, a user can plant a link that points elsewhere and wait for root or a service to write through it. These protections block that whole class of attack.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w fs.protected_hardlinks=1 fs.protected_symlinks=1` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `fs.protected_hardlinks = 1` and `fs.protected_symlinks = 1` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'fs.protected_hardlinks|fs.protected_symlinks' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files.

rules.title: Privileged programs can write core dumps
rules.finding_message: fs.suid_dumpable is not 0 and cores are written to files, so a crashing privileged program can leave its memory, secrets included, on disk. Set it to 0, or send cores to a handler such as systemd-coredump.
rules.explain: When a program with extra rights (setuid, such as passwd or sudo) crashes, its memory can be written to a core file on disk. That memory can hold password hashes, keys or other secrets.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w fs.suid_dumpable=0` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `fs.suid_dumpable = 0` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'fs.suid_dumpable' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files. Or let systemd-coredump store cores safely (`apt install systemd-coredump` on Debian/Ubuntu; Fedora has it).

rules.title: The host forwards IP packets
rules.expression: facts['sysctl.net.ipv4.ip_forward'] == 1 && !('docker' in facts['package.names'] || 'docker-ce' in facts['package.names'] || 'moby-engine' in facts['package.names'] || 'podman' in facts['package.names'] || 'containerd' in facts['package.names'] || 'containerd.io' in facts['package.names'] || 'cri-o' in facts['package.names'] || 'kubelet' in facts['package.names'] || 'docker.service' in facts['service.active'] || 'podman.service' in facts['service.active'] || 'containerd.service' in facts['service.active'] || 'crio.service' in facts['service.active'] || 'kubelet.service' in facts['service.active'])
rules.finding_message: net.ipv4.ip_forward is 1 on a host with no container runtime, so it routes packets between networks. Set it to 0 unless this host is a router.
rules.explain: With forwarding on, the host passes packets between its networks like a router. An attacker on one network, such as guest Wi-Fi, could then reach another through this host.
rules.check: Check first: routers, VM hosts (libvirt NAT), LXD/Incus, k3s/rke2, VPN servers, and WireGuard or Tailscale exit or subnet nodes need it; keep it at 1 there and suppress this finding. On other hosts, run `sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=0` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'net.ipv4.ip_forward' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files.

rules.title: The host sends ICMP redirects
rules.finding_message: The host is not a router but sends ICMP redirects (net.ipv4.conf.all or default send_redirects is 1), which can steer other hosts' traffic. Set both to 0.
rules.explain: ICMP redirects tell other hosts to send their traffic a different way. Only routers need to send them; on other hosts they are a way to misdirect traffic on the LAN.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0 net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects=0` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects = 0` and `net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects = 0` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects|net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files.

rules.title: The host accepts source-routed IPv4 packets
rules.finding_message: net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route is 1: the sender chooses the route, which can bypass filtering. Set it to 0.
rules.explain: Source-routed packets carry their own route, chosen by the sender. Accepting them lets an attacker push traffic past firewalls or make it look like it came along a trusted path.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route=0` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files.

rules.title: The host accepts source-routed IPv6 packets
rules.finding_message: net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route is 1: the sender chooses the route, which can bypass filtering. Set it to 0.
rules.explain: Source-routed IPv6 packets carry their own route, chosen by the sender. Accepting them lets an attacker push traffic past firewalls or make it look like it came along a trusted path.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route=0` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files.

rules.title: The host accepts IPv4 ICMP redirects
rules.finding_message: net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects is 1: another host can change this host's routes. Set it to 0.
rules.explain: An ICMP redirect tells the host to send traffic through a different gateway. Accepting them lets anyone on the LAN quietly route this host's traffic through their own machine.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0 net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects=0` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0` and `net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects|net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files. `sysctl -a | grep accept_redirects` shows each interface's value.

rules.title: The host accepts IPv6 ICMP redirects
rules.finding_message: net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects is 1: another host can change this host's routes. Set it to 0.
rules.explain: An IPv6 redirect tells the host to send traffic through a different gateway. Accepting them lets anyone on the LAN quietly route this host's traffic through their own machine.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects=0 net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects=0` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0` and `net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects|net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files. Each IPv6 interface keeps its own value: also `sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.<iface>.accept_redirects=0`.

rules.title: The host answers broadcast pings
rules.finding_message: net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts is 0: the host answers pings to broadcast addresses, which amplifies floods. Set it to 1.
rules.explain: If the host answers pings sent to a broadcast address, an attacker can send one forged ping and have every such host flood the victim with replies (a smurf attack).
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts=1` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files.

rules.title: SYN cookies are off
rules.finding_message: net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies is 0, so a SYN flood can fill the connection queue. Set it to 1.
rules.explain: A SYN flood sends many half-opened connections to fill the server's queue, so real clients cannot connect. SYN cookies let the kernel keep answering real clients during such a flood.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files.

rules.title: Reverse path filtering is off
rules.finding_message: net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter is 0: packets with spoofed source addresses are accepted. Set it to 1 (strict) or 2 (loose).
rules.explain: Reverse path filtering drops packets whose source address could not have arrived on that interface. Without it, forged packets that claim to come from the inside network are accepted.
rules.check: Run `sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1` to change it now. To keep it after a reboot, put `net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1` in /etc/sysctl.d/90-openvibes.conf and remove other settings of it (`grep -rE 'net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/`), since the file read last wins. `sysctl --system` reloads all files. Use 2 (loose) on hosts with several uplinks or asymmetric routing.

rules.title: /etc/shadow is open to other users
rules.finding_message: /etc/shadow (or its backup /etc/shadow-) can be read by other users or is not owned by root; it holds the password hashes. Make it owned by root with no access for others (0640 or 0000).
rules.explain: /etc/shadow holds every account's password hash. Anyone who can read it can try to crack the passwords offline, and anyone who can write it can set root's password.
rules.check: Fedora/RHEL: `chown root:root /etc/shadow /etc/shadow-; chmod 0000 /etc/shadow /etc/shadow-`. Debian/Ubuntu: `chown root:shadow /etc/shadow /etc/shadow-; chmod 0640 /etc/shadow /etc/shadow-`. These are the stock modes; no restart is needed. If a backup (-) file is missing, ignore that one error.

rules.title: /etc/gshadow is open to other users
rules.finding_message: /etc/gshadow (or its backup /etc/gshadow-) can be read by other users or is not owned by root; it holds group password hashes. Make it owned by root with no access for others.
rules.explain: /etc/gshadow holds group password hashes and the group administrators. Anyone who can read it can try to crack them offline, and anyone who can write it can add themselves to any group.
rules.check: Fedora/RHEL: `chown root:root /etc/gshadow /etc/gshadow-; chmod 0000 /etc/gshadow /etc/gshadow-`. Debian/Ubuntu: `chown root:shadow /etc/gshadow /etc/gshadow-; chmod 0640 /etc/gshadow /etc/gshadow-`. These are the stock modes; no restart is needed. If a backup (-) file is missing, ignore that one error.

rules.title: /etc/passwd or /etc/group can be changed by other users
rules.expression: (facts['file.etc_passwd.mode'] != '' && facts['file.etc_passwd.mode'] != '0644' && facts['file.etc_passwd.mode'] != '0640' && facts['file.etc_passwd.mode'] != '0600' && facts['file.etc_passwd.mode'] != '0444' && facts['file.etc_passwd.mode'] != '0440' && facts['file.etc_passwd.mode'] != '0400') || (facts['file.etc_group.mode'] != '' && facts['file.etc_group.mode'] != '0644' && facts['file.etc_group.mode'] != '0640' && facts['file.etc_group.mode'] != '0600' && facts['file.etc_group.mode'] != '0444' && facts['file.etc_group.mode'] != '0440' && facts['file.etc_group.mode'] != '0400')
rules.finding_message: /etc/passwd or /etc/group has a mode other than 0644 or stricter, such as writable by its group or by others, so an account could give itself root. Make both 0644 root:root.
rules.explain: /etc/passwd and /etc/group list the accounts and groups. If someone other than root can write them, they can give an account uid 0 or add it to an admin group, and so become root.
rules.check: Run `chown root:root /etc/passwd /etc/group && chmod 0644 /etc/passwd /etc/group`. No restart is needed.

rules.title: System cron files can be changed by other users
rules.expression: (facts['file.etc_crontab.mode'] != '' && facts['file.etc_crontab.mode'] != '0644' && facts['file.etc_crontab.mode'] != '0640' && facts['file.etc_crontab.mode'] != '0600' && facts['file.etc_crontab.mode'] != '0444' && facts['file.etc_crontab.mode'] != '0440' && facts['file.etc_crontab.mode'] != '0400') || (facts['file.etc_cron_d.mode'] != '' && facts['file.etc_cron_d.mode'] != '0755' && facts['file.etc_cron_d.mode'] != '0750' && facts['file.etc_cron_d.mode'] != '0700' && facts['file.etc_cron_d.mode'] != '0555' && facts['file.etc_cron_d.mode'] != '0550' && facts['file.etc_cron_d.mode'] != '0500')
rules.finding_message: /etc/crontab or /etc/cron.d has a mode that lets more than root change it (accepted: 0644 or stricter for the file, 0755 or stricter for the directory), so others could schedule commands as root. Make them writable by root only.
rules.explain: Jobs in /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d run as root on a schedule. If anyone else can change them, they can make the host run their command as root.
rules.check: Run `chown root:root /etc/crontab /etc/cron.d`, `chmod 0644 /etc/crontab` and `chmod 0755 /etc/cron.d` (0600 and 0700 are stricter and also fine). cron picks up the change itself.

rules.title: The boot loader configuration is readable by all users
rules.finding_message: grub.cfg can be read by every user; it can hold the boot loader password hash and kernel options. Make it 0600 (or 0400) root:root.
rules.explain: grub.cfg holds the boot menu and kernel options, and can hold the boot loader password hash. Readable by every user, it hands out that hash for offline cracking.
rules.check: Fedora/RHEL: `chown root:root /boot/grub2/grub.cfg && chmod 0600 /boot/grub2/grub.cfg`. Debian/Ubuntu: the same on /boot/grub/grub.cfg. On Debian/Ubuntu, update-grub writes the file as 0444 again when no boot password is set, so a kernel update can undo this.

rules.title: An account other than root has uid 0
rules.finding_message: An account other than root has uid 0, so it has every power root has. Remove it or give it its own uid.
rules.explain: Any account with uid 0 is root, whatever its name. A second uid-0 account is a classic backdoor and is easy to miss because it does not look like root.
rules.check: First make sure you can get in as root or a sudo user. List them with `awk -F: '$3==0 {print $1}' /etc/passwd`; if you did not create the extra one on purpose, treat the host as possibly compromised. If it is the only uid-0 account (root was renamed), rename it back to root instead. Otherwise usermod and userdel refuse it, so run `vipw` and change only its uid (third field) to a free one, or delete its line; never edit root's line. Then run `vipw -s` to match /etc/shadow, and `pwck` to check.

rules.title: An account has an empty password
rules.finding_message: An account has an empty password field in /etc/shadow; depending on PAM it can log in without a password. Lock it (passwd -l) or set a password.
rules.explain: An account with an empty password field may log in with no password at all, depending on PAM settings (the nullok option). Anyone who knows its name could get in.
rules.check: List them with `awk -F: '$2=="" {print $1}' /etc/shadow`. Lock each with `passwd -l <name>`, or set a password with `passwd <name>`.

rules.title: A system account has a login shell
rules.finding_message: A system account (uid 1 to 999) has a login shell, so it can be used to log in interactively. Set its shell to /usr/sbin/nologin unless it needs one.
rules.explain: System accounts run services and should never log in. If one has a real shell, a leaked password or a flaw in its service can turn into an interactive login.
rules.check: List them with `awk -F: '$3>0 && $3<1000 && $7 !~ /(nologin|false)$/ {print $1, $7}' /etc/passwd`. For each that does not need a shell, run `usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin <name>`. Some do need one, such as postgres or an account that runs git or backups over SSH; leave those and suppress the finding.

rules.title: Passwords are hashed with a weak method
rules.expression: facts['login_defs.encrypt_method'] != '' && !(facts['login_defs.encrypt_method'] == 'sha512' || facts['login_defs.encrypt_method'] == 'Sha512' || facts['login_defs.encrypt_method'] == 'SHA512' || facts['login_defs.encrypt_method'] == 'yescrypt' || facts['login_defs.encrypt_method'] == 'Yescrypt' || facts['login_defs.encrypt_method'] == 'YESCRYPT')
rules.finding_message: /etc/login.defs sets ENCRYPT_METHOD to something other than SHA512 or YESCRYPT, so new password hashes are easier to crack. Set ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512 or YESCRYPT.
rules.explain: New passwords are stored as hashes made with this method. Older methods such as MD5 or DES are fast to crack, so a stolen /etc/shadow gives up the passwords quickly.
rules.check: In /etc/login.defs set `ENCRYPT_METHOD YESCRYPT` (the default on current Fedora, Debian and Ubuntu) or `ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512`. Existing passwords keep their old hash until they are changed: `chage -d 0 <name>` makes a user pick a new one at the next login.

rules.title: Passwords may be shorter than 12 characters
rules.finding_message: pam_pwquality checks passwords but allows fewer than 12 characters (minlen, default 8). Set minlen = 12 or more in /etc/security/pwquality.conf.
rules.explain: Short passwords are guessed or cracked quickly. pam_pwquality checks new passwords on this host but lets them be shorter than 12 characters.
rules.check: Set `minlen = 12` (or more) in /etc/security/pwquality.conf or a file in /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/. If a pam_pwquality.so line in /etc/pam.d/ has its own `minlen=`, change it there too. It applies to the next password change; nothing needs restarting.

rules.title: Failed logins never lock an account
rules.finding_message: No PAM stack uses pam_faillock (or deny is 0), so passwords can be guessed without limit. Enable pam_faillock with deny = 5 or fewer.
rules.explain: Without a lockout, a program can try passwords against local logins, su and sudo without limit. pam_faillock locks an account for a while after several failures.
rules.check: Keep a root shell open while testing. Fedora/RHEL: `authselect enable-feature with-faillock`. Debian/Ubuntu, in /etc/pam.d/common-auth put `auth required pam_faillock.so preauth` before pam_unix, `auth [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail` right after it, and add 1 to pam_unix's `success=N` (1 becomes 2 if stock) and to any other jump that crosses the new line. Add `account required pam_faillock.so` to common-account; pam-auth-update may rewrite both. In /etc/security/faillock.conf set `deny = 5`, `unlock_time = 900`; then anyone can lock a user out. `faillock --user <name> --reset` unlocks.

rules.title: Avahi (mDNS) is enabled
rules.finding_message: avahi-daemon is enabled: it announces the host and its services on the local network. Disable it on servers (systemctl disable --now avahi-daemon.service avahi-daemon.socket).
rules.explain: avahi-daemon announces the host's name and services (printers, shares, SSH) to the local network and answers queries from it. On a server this mostly helps an attacker map the network, and avahi has had remotely reachable bugs.
rules.check: Run `systemctl disable --now avahi-daemon.service avahi-daemon.socket`. To stop other packages turning it back on, `systemctl mask avahi-daemon.service avahi-daemon.socket`. Desktops that find printers this way can keep it.

rules.title: A rarely used network protocol module is loaded
rules.expression: 'dccp' in facts['kernel.modules.loaded'] || 'sctp' in facts['kernel.modules.loaded'] || 'rds' in facts['kernel.modules.loaded'] || 'tipc' in facts['kernel.modules.loaded']
rules.finding_message: A rarely used network protocol (dccp, sctp, rds or tipc) is loaded; these have had remotely reachable kernel bugs. Unload it and block it in /etc/modprobe.d unless it is needed.
rules.explain: DCCP, SCTP, RDS and TIPC are network protocols few hosts use. The kernel loads them on demand when a program asks, and each has had kernel bugs that let an attacker take control.
rules.check: Create /etc/modprobe.d/openvibes-rare-net.conf with the lines `install dccp /bin/false`, `install sctp /bin/false`, `install rds /bin/false` and `install tipc /bin/false`, then unload the loaded one with `modprobe -r <name>` (or reboot). Leave out sctp if you run software that uses it, such as telecom or some cluster tools.

rules.title: SELinux is disabled
rules.finding_message: SELinux is disabled on a Fedora/RHEL-family host, which removes its confinement of services. Enable it (SELINUX=enforcing) and relabel.
rules.explain: SELinux confines each service to what it needs, so a hacked web server cannot read SSH keys or other services' data. Disabled, a flaw in any service has the full reach of the user it runs as.
rules.check: In /etc/selinux/config set `SELINUX=permissive`, remove any `selinux=0` from the kernel command line (`grubby --update-kernel ALL --remove-args selinux`), run `touch /.autorelabel` and reboot; the relabel takes a while. Check `ausearch -m avc -ts boot` for denials, then set `SELINUX=enforcing` and run `setenforce 1`.

rules.title: SELinux only logs
rules.finding_message: SELinux is permissive on a Fedora/RHEL-family host: it logs denials but blocks nothing. Set it to enforcing.
rules.explain: In permissive mode SELinux only logs what it would block. Services lose its protection while it still looks switched on.
rules.check: Look for denials first: `ausearch -m avc -ts recent` (often fixed with `restorecon -Rv <path>` or a `setsebool -P` boolean). Then `setenforce 1` for now, and `SELINUX=enforcing` in /etc/selinux/config for reboots. If the kernel command line has `enforcing=0`, remove it: `grubby --update-kernel ALL --remove-args enforcing`.

rules.title: AppArmor is disabled
rules.finding_message: AppArmor is disabled on a Debian/Ubuntu host, which removes its confinement of services. Enable it (apparmor=1 on the kernel command line, and the service).
rules.explain: AppArmor limits what each confined program (for example CUPS, libvirt or snaps) may read and run. Disabled, a flaw in one of those programs has the full reach of the user it runs as.
rules.check: Install it if missing (`apt install apparmor apparmor-utils`). In /etc/default/grub, remove `apparmor=0` from GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX (or an `lsm=` or `security=` setting that leaves AppArmor out), run `update-grub`, `systemctl enable apparmor`, and reboot. `aa-status` shows the loaded profiles.
